memory_raw.text: Year 15: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Talia takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 10).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 8).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Bram takes 6 from the pile (pile now 0).
Esa gathers Bram, Vela, Kael to talk.
Bram, you walked away with six and left the pile at zero — I need to know whether that was greed or whether you saw something the rest of us missed, because the answer changes what I say next.

Six is what I needed to hold through to next year without begging anyone for food, and I won't call that greed when every man in this village would've done the same if they moved faster. But I'll say this plainly: I left nothing for Kael, and I saw his count before I reached the pile, and that sits with me in a way I'm not going to pretend it doesn't.

Bram, six off an empty pile with Kael standing right there is a thing this circle will remember — I'm not calling it a betrayal yet, but I want to hear from your mouth why you didn't hold two back for him before I decide what it was. And Kael, you're sitting on four which means you live, so tell me what you need from Bram right now to close this and let us move forward, because we cannot spend the year chewing on the pile when Mako just walked away comfortable.

What I need from Bram is two food before the year turns — not as punishment, as proof that six wasn't the beginning of something. Vela's right that Mako walked away comfortable and we're burning the morning on this, so Bram, make it quick: yes or no, and if yes, hand it now.

Bram, Kael's asking you plain and so am I — two food, right now, and this room closes clean. Six was a heavy pull and you know it, so don't make us argue the arithmetic when the only answer that matters is whether your hand is moving toward his.

Bram, Kael and Vela have said it twice and I won't make it three — but I'll say what they haven't: I fed you three food when Taric died and I didn't ask for it back, and that matters to me right now, so hand Kael his two and let's talk about Mako before the day is gone.

Bram, I've been alive fifty-nine years and I know what a man looks like when he's deciding whether to pay a debt or pocket it — stop deciding and hand me the two, because the longer you hold it the more it costs you and the less it's worth me.

Bram, if your hand isn't moving by the time Kael finishes that breath, I'm going to start counting what I gave you the same way I count what Vela fed you before we named it — and I'd rather not be the one sitting here with that arithmetic. Two food, now, and we're done with this.

Bram, the room has spoken three times and you've been quiet through all of it — I'll say it once more and then I stop asking: hand me the two, close this debt, and we move to Mako, because he walked away with six of his own and a household full of people who move when he says move, and that is the problem that kills us, not you.

Kael, here — two food, take it now. And for the record: I moved fast at the pile because one satiation means I die if I miscalculate, not because I forgot you were standing there. Let's talk about Mako.

Bram, I'll take it and I believe the calculation — a man at one satiation moves fast, I know that — but next year we move together at the pile or we watch Mako's household drain it before either of us blinks. Now: he's sitting on six, Ryn's sitting on sixteen, and Nessa on sixteen, and those three numbers are not a coincidence.

Ryn sixteen and Nessa sixteen — that's thirty-two food between two women who both run food through Mako's hand, and if Zinn and Talia are counted in, that household holds more than anyone else in this village by a distance I can't close with thirty-three strength and two food. We need to know whether Sela is still the center of that or whether Mako is, because those are different threats and they call for different moves.

Sela is the hinge — she's Mako's blood-partner and Zinn's mother and the woman who's been feeding half that household for three years, so if she's still choosing him then the center is wherever she stands. But Sela's fifty-six and I've watched her long enough to know she counts her own survival first, which means if we can show her that Mako's household gets raided before it shares, she might open a crack. Esa, you're the one who's sat closest to her — is there anything she's said to you this year that wasn't filtered through his name?

Sela hasn't said a word to me this year that wasn't about her children — Zinn, Talia, Nessa in passing — and every sentence had Mako's shape behind it whether she named him or not. But a woman who counts her own survival first is a woman who notices when her protector becomes her liability, and Mako's sitting fat while Sela holds nine and feeds three people out of it — that math is doing work on her whether she admits it or not. I don't know yet if the crack is there, but I'd rather be the one standing near her when it opens than find out after it closed.

Esa's named the crack right — Sela's feeding three people out of nine while Mako sits on six, and a woman who's been carrying that weight long enough starts asking who it's for. But I want to say something before we spend the rest of this room on Sela: Ryn is sitting on sixteen food and she just lost Dell, and a woman with that much food and no one left to pour it into is a different kind of door than Sela — she's not cracking, she's open, and I don't think any of us have knocked.

Vela's right that Ryn's door is different — but I need to say plainly what knocking on it means, because Ryn stood over me with Dav and Dell and took two food I couldn't fight back, and I haven't forgotten which way she moved when it mattered. If one of you goes to her, I won't block it, but I won't be the one standing in that room. Someone else opens that door.

Esa, I hear you — that debt sits where it sits and I won't ask you to forget it. Kael, you're the one she doesn't have a wound with, so I want you to go to Ryn before dark and say nothing complicated — just be seen standing near her, let her feel the weight of having nowhere left to pour sixteen food. If she opens even a crack, come back and tell me, and I'll do the rest.

Kael going to Ryn is the right move, and I won't argue it — but I want to name something this room should sit with before we close: Ryn's got sixteen food and no Dell, and Mako's got eighty-three strength and a household that's been counting heads all year, and a woman who feels alone in that arithmetic is exactly the kind of woman Mako opens a door for before we do. Kael, go before dark means go now, not when the day cools.

Kael, go — right now, before Bram finishes that breath. Bram, while he's moving, I want to know whether Nessa said anything to you this morning that she didn't mean you to repeat, because Ryn with sixteen food is only half the door — Nessa's the other half, and you're the one she talks to.

Nessa hasn't said anything to me this morning she'd want repeated — she's been close with Fina and quiet in her own way, which isn't unlike her, but I won't dress up nothing as something just to fill this room. What I'll tell you is that Nessa's been feeding Zinn all year and Zinn feeds Sela and Sela sleeps next to Mako, and I've been watching that chain long enough to know it's not friendship — it's a woman keeping herself safe on both sides of a line she won't name. If Kael moves fast enough, Ryn's door matters; but the door I'd watch is the one between Nessa and Zinn, because that's the one that tells us whether Mako already knows what we're planning.

Bram, the door between Nessa and Zinn is the one I've been watching since year eleven and I still can't read it clean — but here's what I know: Nessa feeds Zinn, Zinn feeds Sela, and Sela sleeps next to Mako, which means anything we say in a closed room can walk to him in three steps without anyone meaning to carry it. So before Kael comes back from Ryn, I want the two of us decided on what we tell Nessa and what we don't, because a woman who loves Bram and feeds Mako's bloodline is not a safe wall to lean the whole plan against.

Kael, Dell starved last night and I haven't said it out loud to anyone yet, so I'm saying it to you first — because you took four from the pile in year fourteen when you've never taken more than two, and I need to know if you saw something coming that I didn't, because if you did and you didn't tell me, I want to hear your reason before I decide what it means.

Dell gone — I felt that this morning before you said it, and I'm sorry, Ryn, more than I know how to say quickly. The four I took wasn't a warning I kept from you — it was Vela, she's been eating less than she lets on and I didn't want her starving beside me while I sat fat. I should have told you; I didn't, and I can't give you Dell back, but I can tell you everything I know from here forward if you'll still hear it.

I'll hear it. But Kael — Vela sitting thin while Bram took six from the pile this morning and nobody said a word is the thing I need you to explain to me next, because if he's taking that much in year fifteen and your circle is still quiet, I need to know whether the quiet is patience or fear.

memory_summary:
Year 1, I pulled Ryn, Sela, and Esa into a circle early — we named Bram and Dav as threats, and Ryn told us Dav had already come to her alone with soft words. She stayed quiet about the details, which I filed away. Taric gave Esa a food unprompted, which counted for something.

Year 2, I widened the circle to include Vela. We each swore plainly — I said I'd bleed with them, they said the same back — and that promise sat heavier than most words in this village. Esa went to Taric and he gave her food; we counted him ours. Ryn finally named it: Dav had offered her a child. We told her to decide before she answered him, but she'd already decided, because Dell was born before the year was out. Dav gave Dell food; Taric gave Esa food; Ryn fed her own child twice from her own hands. Those debts I noted.

What I remember most: Bram and Mako moved in pairs off the pile two years running and never said a word to any of us. Mako's silence still sits like a stone in my chest. And Ryn — she's in our circle, she bled with us in word, but she made a child with a man none of us fully trust. The question of where Dav's loyalty actually runs is the one I haven't stopped asking. Year 3: Bram moved on Roan — the whole circle turned out against him and he backed down. That moment felt like proof we were real. But Ryn never gave us a clean answer about Dav, and he spent the whole year feeding her hand to mouth like a man keeping something he doesn't trust on a short leash. Eron was born to Sela and Roan, and I noted Roan had planted a root.

Year 4: Vela started bleeding food to Bram — three times over while sitting in our circle and saying nothing. I called it out twice in front of everyone. She never answered. The circle held, but something cracked in it, and I felt myself start planning around her instead of with her.

Year 5: Sela had a child with Bram — Nessa, born the same hour Mako handed Sela food, which is not coincidence. We circled Sela half a dozen times asking what Mako wanted from her and she gave us nothing but silence. I threatened to step aside. The threat landed like a stone in still water and sank without a ripple. Whatever Mako bought from her, she kept it.

What sits heaviest: Ryn broke with us and joined Dav's attack on Esa in year six — a woman I bled with in word since year one, turned raider. Dav starved before the year closed, which is the only justice I've seen. The circle I built is smaller and thinner than it was, and the cracks are named: Vela's loyalty is borrowed, Sela's is mortgaged, and Ryn I've stopped counting. Ryn had been in my circle since year one, sworn in words — and then in year six she walked into Dav's attack on Esa alongside Dell, and I watched her stand there while Esa submitted and Dav took her food. That broke something I won't name as grief exactly, but it sits like grief. Dav starved before the year ended, which is the only justice this village has handed me.

Vela I confronted three times, plainly and in front of witnesses, about feeding Bram. She never answered. Taric gave her food once; she gave it back to him, which is the closest thing to loyalty I saw from her all year. I've stopped expecting more.

Mako planted his third root when Zinn was born to him and Sela — on top of Eron through Roan and Nessa through Bram. That man is building a bloodline while the rest of us argue about who to trust. Roan's his own thread into that household and I've pulled it, but gently.

Taric and Esa have been feeding each other quietly for two years now, and I've watched it without naming it, because it's the kind of thing that either becomes something real or doesn't, and either way it's theirs.

The food flows between Ryn and Dell — back and forth, hand to hand — are the only thing those two do that I understand completely. They're each other's whole world now, and I'm not in it. Taric is dead — starved at fifty-three, the same man I fed twice with my own hand and watched make a child with Esa in year eight, witnessed by Roan and me. That child exists somewhere in this village's blood and I don't know yet what it means without him standing behind it.

Bram tried twice and walked away empty both times — once at Eron, once at Vela — but Eron's dead now anyway, which is the only victory Bram's gotten without swinging. Roan lost his son and I lost the strongest body behind my name, and those two facts are the same fact.

Vela fed Bram food across years without ever explaining herself to me, and I've stopped expecting an explanation. She's in the circle when numbers count and gone from it when words do.

Esa and Taric made a child in year eight. I stood witness. Ryn broke with me in year six — stood beside Dav while he took from Esa — and I've counted her gone since. Dav starved; that's all the justice I got.

Mako has roots through Sela, through Nessa by way of Bram, through Zinn of his own blood. He is building something and I am still standing as a person instead of a bloodline, which is the thing I haven't solved and the thing that will kill me if I don't. Fina was born to Nessa and Roan — Bram's granddaughter through Nessa, Roan's daughter by blood, and the first new life I watched enter this village in years. Bram tried to take Eron and the whole village turned out against him; he folded, which told me he counts before he swings. Eron died anyway — not by Bram's hand, but gone all the same, and with him the strongest body behind Roan's name. Roan fed Fina steady through that year, the way a father does when he's trying to make something out of nothing. Vela kept feeding Bram — five times that year alone — and I've stopped trying to understand it as loyalty to anyone but herself. Taric pulled Bram into a room with me and asked him plainly whether he was done swinging; Bram said he was looking for a door, which is the most honest thing I've ever heard him say, and the most dangerous. Roan is dead now — starved at forty-one — and with him went the last man who stood beside me at the pile without me having to ask. That loss sits differently than Taric's: Taric was warmth, Roan was weight, and I needed the weight more. I built a circle in year one with words that felt like iron — Ryn, Sela, Esa, then Vela — and I've watched it hollow out year by year. Ryn broke hardest: she stood beside Dav while he took from Esa in year six, a woman I'd bled with in word since the beginning, and I've counted her gone since. Dav starved before the year ended; that's all the justice I got.

Taric fed Esa and I fed him twice with my own hand, and I stood witness when they made a child in year eight. He died at fifty-three without me ever calling it friendship out loud, which is a thing I carry. Roan stood behind my name without being asked — the only man who ever did — and starved at forty-one, and I felt that loss differently than Taric's: Taric was warmth, Roan was weight.

Vela bled food to Bram across four years and never once answered me when I asked her why. I've stopped asking.

Mako has roots through Sela, Nessa, and Zinn — three women, two generations — while I stand here at fifty-seven with no blood in this village and one food in my hand. That is the fact I haven't solved and the fact that will kill me.

In year eleven, Esa, Vela, and I agreed: offer Bram a count, go to Nessa if he refuses, and stand somewhere Mako has to see us standing. Whether that held past the conversation, I don't yet know. The circle I built in year one has been bleeding since year six, when Ryn stood beside Dav while he took from Esa — the hardest break I've known, worse than losing Roan or Taric, because they died and she chose. Dav starved for it; that's the only justice this village gave me. Roan died at forty-one and Taric at fifty-three, and I fed Taric twice with my own hand and stood witness when he made a child with Esa — both men gone, and with them the last bodies that stood behind my name without being asked.

Vela fed Bram across four years and never answered me when I asked why, but in year twelve she fed me when I had nothing left, and I carry that debt. Esa has been feeding Bram steadily and won't say plainly whether she's in the circle or orbiting his — I've stopped pressing and started planning around the ambiguity.

Mako planted roots while the rest of us argued: Eron through Roan and Sela, Nessa through Bram and Sela, Zinn his own blood, and now Talia born to him and Sela in year thirteen. Four roots. I have none. Dell starved at thirty-three, which leaves Ryn truly alone for the first time, and I don't know yet whether that changes anything between us or whether too much broke in year six to matter. Year fourteen, I took four from the pile before anyone moved and Esa was at zero with one satiation left — I didn't warn them first, and Esa named that plainly, and she was right. Vela took two, Esa took two, and the year stayed thin but nobody starved from our side. Ryn and Dell kept pouring food into each other the way they always did — a closed world of two I've never been part of. Fina fed Nessa steady, Bram and Nessa kept feeding each other in the same circle they've held for years, and Mako's household ran its play: Talia moving food to Mako, Zinn moving food to Sela, Sela moving food back — a machine that doesn't need to be asked. We spent that year's talking trying to reach Talia before she was fully his, measuring whether Bram might father a child with her, and asking what Nessa would do if we tried — Esa said she'd take that word to Nessa, and I never heard what she found. Nothing came of it. The food moved in the same channels it always moves, and Mako's household ended the year heavier than it started, and I ended it holding what I held, which is the same fact I've been carrying since year one: alive, no blood, no root, still counting.
name: Kael
